title: Sequence representations
goals: Encode an ordered sequence with an explicit vocabulary
Use padding and a mask without inventing real events
Identify information lost by counts unknown symbols and truncation

prerequisite.prompt: Why can two different image regions have the same pooled maximum?
prerequisite.answer: Pooling discards detail. A maximum can preserve the largest value while losing its location and the other values; identical summaries do not imply identical inputs.

vocabulary: An ordered list of elements in which positions can matter
A numerical identifier assigned to a symbol by a vocabulary
Placeholder positions added to make stored sequences the same length
A list marking which stored positions are real inputs and which are placeholders

blocks.text: Use fictional robot event logs whose symbols are GO, TURN and STOP. The task asks whether the final real event is STOP. This is a representation exercise, not a claim that an event log proves a robot is safe. GO then STOP and STOP then GO contain the same symbols but have different final events.

headers: Counts in GO TURN STOP order

blocks.text: A count vector discards order, so no deterministic rule using only the first two count vectors can distinguish their answers. A sequence of IDs preserves order if we retain each position. Declare the vocabulary: PAD = 0, UNK = 1, GO = 2, TURN = 3 and STOP = 4. PAD is reserved for added storage positions; UNK represents a real but unrecognised symbol.

IDs are names, not measured amounts. STOP having ID 4 does not make it twice as much as GO with ID 2. Changing the vocabulary requires changing every consumer consistently. Do not interpret numerical distance between IDs as semantic similarity.

Store each log in four positions, padding on the right. A mask value 1 marks a real position and 0 marks padding. The encoder rejects empty logs, logs longer than four, and literal reserved markers. Other unrecognised symbols become UNK and still receive mask 1.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: The code assumes a list of symbol strings and uses exact spelling. It does not fit a vocabulary from data. If a future project fits vocabulary choices or frequency cutoffs, derive those choices from training data and apply the saved encoding consistently to validation and final cases.

lesson.title: Read the mask before the final position

blocks.title: A padded log still has two real events
blocks.caption: The final stored slot is padding. For this right-padded contiguous mask, the real length is the mask sum, and the final real event is at length minus one. A different masking layout would need a different indexing rule.

blocks.label: Encode TURN STOP, give its mask and real length, then identify the final real position and its ID. Why would reading stored position 3 give the wrong event?

lesson.title: Use masks in the actual computation

blocks.text: A mask must affect a calculation to protect it from padding. Suppose real sensor values are [2, 4], stored as [2, 4, 0, 0] with mask [1, 1, 0, 0]. The masked mean is (2 + 4) / 2 = 3. Averaging all four slots gives 1.5. Unlike arbitrary token IDs, these sensor values are measurements for which a mean is meaningful.

Measured zero must remain real: values [0, 4, 0, 0] with mask [1, 1, 0, 0] have mean 2. Removing every zero would incorrectly give 4. The mask distinguishes a measured zero from a storage placeholder. An all-zero mask has no real values; reject it or follow an explicitly defined empty-input policy instead of dividing by zero.

Storing ordered IDs makes order available but does not guarantee a later model uses it. A computation that sums token counts or averages position-independent vectors can lose order again. Trace what the whole procedure reads, not just what the input format could preserve.

WAIT STOP and PAUSE STOP both become [1, 4, 0, 0] with the same mask. UNK retains a real position but loses the identity of the unrecognised symbol. The final-event task can still answer Yes for both because the last real ID is STOP. A final real UNK would require an unknown result or another documented policy when the intended event cannot be determined.

blocks.label: A log GO TURN GO TURN STOP is cut to its first four events before encoding. What happens to the final-event answer? Explain why the lesson encoder rejects the original log instead of silently truncating it.

blocks.text: The full log ends in STOP, while the retained prefix ends in TURN. Truncation changes the evidence needed for this task. Save the original length and any truncation policy in a real experiment, and test the consequences. Next week introduces embeddings while preserving the distinction between identifiers and learned vectors.

workbook.title: Encode and recover the final event
workbook.prompt: Encode GO TURN STOP using the lesson vocabulary and four positions. Give its mask, real length and final real event.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: IDs are [2, 3, 4, 0], mask [1, 1, 1, 0], real length 3 and final real event STOP at position 2.

workbook.title: Expose an order collision
workbook.prompt: Give two logs made of exactly GO, TURN and STOP once each that have equal count vectors but different answers to whether the final event is STOP.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: For example GO TURN STOP and STOP TURN GO both have count vector [1, 1, 1]. The first answer is Yes and the second No. Counts alone cannot distinguish them.

workbook.title: Separate unknown from padding
workbook.prompt: Encode WAIT GO. Which positions are real? Compare it with PAUSE GO, and state what information the encoding loses.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both encode as [1, 2, 0, 0] with mask [1, 1, 0, 0]. Positions 0 and 1 are real. UNK at position 0 loses whether the symbol was WAIT or PAUSE; padding is only at positions 2 and 3.

workbook.title: Apply a fresh schema independently
workbook.prompt: Use PAD = 0, UNK = 1, OPEN = 2, CLOSE = 3, CHECK = 4 and five stored positions. Encode OPEN CHECK CLOSE and give its mask and final real position. Separately, sensor values [0, 6, 3, 0, 0] have that same mask. Calculate their masked mean and the incorrect mean over all five slots.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: IDs [2, 4, 3, 0, 0], mask [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]; final real position 2 contains CLOSE. Masked sensor mean is (0 + 6 + 3) / 3 = 3. Unmasked mean is 9 / 5 = 1.8. The measured zero must count in the denominator.

workbook.title: Audit length and empty input
workbook.prompt: The encoder receives five events ending in STOP, then an empty log. What should it do under the lesson contract? Why should a program not simply crop the first and assume a final event for the second?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It rejects both: one exceeds four real events and the other has none. Cropping can remove the final event and change the task answer. An empty log has no final real position; the program needs an explicit policy rather than an invented event.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions. Arrange event cards physically before using IDs. Keep token identifiers separate from the sensor measurements used for meaningful mean calculations. The encoder is a fixed classroom schema, not a learned language model. All indexing is zero-based and all masks in the examples are contiguous right-padding masks.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve representation collisions and compare GO STOP with STOP GO.
Declare the vocabulary and task, then complete W1 and W2.
Trace the encoder, including a real unknown event and its mask.
Use W3 to distinguish lost unknown identity from artificial padding.
Complete the guided final-position calculation and compare stored versus real length.
Calculate masked sensor means, including a measured zero, and explain the empty-mask boundary.
Collect W4 independently, checking the new vocabulary and five-position layout.
Use W5 and the exit response to audit truncation, then administer the fresh retry.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: TURN STOP becomes IDs [3, 4, 0, 0] and mask [1, 1, 0, 0]. Length is 2, so final real position is 1 with ID 4, STOP. Position 3 is PAD. Exit: the full five-event log answers Yes, but its first four events end in TURN and answer No. Rejection makes the unsupported length visible and avoids silently changing the question.
misconceptions: Larger token IDs mean more of a concept
IDs identify symbols; their arithmetic sizes have no declared semantic meaning.
A measured zero can be real; the mask determines which positions contribute.
A mask automatically fixes every model computation
The relevant operation must actually use the mask, and later aggregation can still discard order.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires IDs [2, 4, 3, 0, 0], mask [1, 1, 1, 0, 0], final index 2, masked mean 3 and unmasked mean 1.8. Fresh retry: use the same five-position vocabulary for CHECK OPEN. IDs are [4, 2, 0, 0, 0], mask [1, 1, 0, 0, 0], final index 1 is OPEN. Sensor values [8, 0, 0, 0, 0] with that mask have mean 4, not 8 or 1.6.
teacher.support: Provide a ledger with position, original symbol, ID and mask. Use separate coloured or labelled cards for real unknowns and placeholders without relying on colour alone. Extension: enumerate all logs of length one through four over GO, TURN and STOP, verify encode-and-decode recovery, and find count-vector collisions with different final-event answers.
